The second assault, on the night of 9th June, is graphically described in _Reminiscences of a Subaltern_:—“At ten o’clock at night, 200 men moved forward to the assault, Dyas leading the advance. He made a circuit until he came exactly opposite to the breach instead of entering the ditch as before; a sheep-path, which he remembered in the evening while he and Major MacGeechy made their observations, served to guide them to the part of the glacis in front of the breach. Arrived at this spot, the detachment descended the ditch, and found themselves at the foot of the breach; but here an unlooked-for event stopped their further progress, and would have been in itself sufficient to have caused the failure of the attack. The ladders were entrusted to a party composed of a foreign corps in our pay, called ‘the Chasseurs Britanniques’; these men, the moment they reached the glacis, glad to rid themselves of their load, flung the ladders into the ditch, instead of sliding them between the palisadoes; they fell across them, and so stuck fast, and being made of heavy green wood, it was next to impossible to _move_, much less place them upright against the breach, and almost all the storming party were massacred in the attempt. Placed in a situation so frightful, it required a man of the most determined character to continue the attack. Every officer of the detachment had fallen, Major MacGeechy one of the first; and at this moment Dyas and about five-and-twenty men were all that remained of the 200. Undismayed by these circumstances, the soldiers persevered, and Dyas, although wounded and bleeding, succeeded in disentangling one ladder, and placing it against what was considered to be the breach, it was speedily mounted, but upon arriving at the top of the ladder, instead of the _breach_, it was found to be a _stone wall_ that had been constructed in the night, and which completely cut off all communication between the ditch and the bastion, so that when the men reached the top of this wall, they were, in effect, as far from the breach as if they had been in their own batteries. From this faithful detail it is evident that the soldiers did as much as possible to ensure success, and that failure was owing to a combination of untoward circumstances over which the troops had no control. Nineteen men were all that escaped.” The gallantry of Ensign Joseph Dyas was proclaimed to the world in Wellington’s account of the two assaults of San Christoval, but for all that a grateful War Office allowed him to remain a subaltern for ten years longer!

“I know a man of whom ’tis truly said He bravely twice a storming party led, And volunteered both times; now here’s the rub, The gallant fellow still remains a sub.”

Chesney, the able author of _Waterloo Lectures_ in commenting on the steadfast manner in which the British Guards faced the advancing Imperial Guards on the summit of the hill, says: “While on their left, Colborne, peerless among all the brave men who led Wellington’s battalions, coolly formed in line the 52nd, and without other prompting than that of his own genius for battle, advanced against their flank.” Created Baron Seaton, of Seaton, Devon, 14th Dec., 1839. Footnote 2:

The following memoir of Col. Jones’s services appeared in the _United Service Journal_ for 1837:—“Nov. 12th, on Lake Erie, Upper Canada, Lt.-Col. Arthur Jones, C.B., late of the 71st Highland L.I. This officer was appointed Ensign 36th Foot, 1st Jan., 1795; Lt. 71st Foot 5th Oct., 1795; Capt., 24th March, 1803; Maj., 22nd June, 1809; and Bt. Lt.-Col., 4th June, 1814. He served at Madras from his first appointment to October, 1797, when his regiment embarked for Europe. In August, 1805, he sailed, with the expedition under Lt. Gen. Sir D. Baird, for the Cape of Good Hope; he was present with the regt. at the action on the 8th Jan., 1806; and also at the surrender of the town and castle of Cape Town on the 10th. He embarked at the Cape in April following, with his regt., on the expedition to South America, under Gen. Beresford. On the 25th June, the landing of this small force was effected at the point of Quilmes, up the River Plate, without opposition. He was present in the affairs of the 26th and 27th, which terminated in the surrender of the city of Buenos Ayres to the British; and was with the troops employed in dispersing the enemy from the vicinity of the city, on the 1st August; at the defending of the city on the 10th, 11th, and 12th, when the British were obliged to capitulate, and become prisoners of war; and was marched, as such, a considerable distance into the interior of the country. He next served with the army in Portugal, and was present at the action of Roleia, and battle of Vimiero. He served under the late Sir John Moore in Spain; was present the whole of that campaign, and at the battle of Corunna. He embarked in July, 1809, on the expedition to the Scheldt, and was present at the siege of Flushing; he returned with his regt. to England in December, and in May, 1810, was ordered to join the 2nd batt. in Scotland; and shortly after the command of the batt. devolved on him. In Jan., 1814, he proceeded to join the 1st batt. in Spain, landed at St. Sebastian, and marched in charge of a detachment for the 2nd division of the army, which he joined in Aire on the 10th of March, and served with it in the different operations that took place against the enemy from that period until a short time after the battle of Toulouse, 10th April, 1814. In Feb., 1815, he embarked with the 71st Light Infantry for North America, but was countermanded, and they proceeded in April to Belgium, and he was present with it at the battle of Waterloo. He remained with the regt., which formed part of the Army of Occupation, until October, 1818, when he embarked with it for England, and for Ireland in May, 1822. The command of the regt. devolved on him in May, 1824, when he embarked with it for North America, and was promoted lt.-col., 2nd June, 1825; he remained in command of the regt. till June, 1831. Lt.-Col. Jones was wounded when capt. at the battle of Vimiero; and wounded severely when bt. lt.-col. at the battle of Waterloo, late in the evening. For his services, and particularly for his conduct at Waterloo, stated by Maj.-Gen. Sir F. Adam (then Commander of the 3rd British Light Brigade) in a letter to the Duke of Wellington, and from his Grace’s recommendation in consequence, Lt.-Col. Jones was appointed a Companion of the Bath.”

The Cameron Highlanders were raised in Jan., 1794, by Lt.-Gen. Sir Alan Cameron, K.C.B. (then Maj. Cameron), who was their first colonel. The officers were mostly selected from the half-pay list, and had served, like their colonel, in the American war. The regt. served during the campaign in Holland, and the mortality was so great that, in 1799, this Scotch regt. had to be again raised. The call for officers and men was nobly responded to by the Clan Cameron:—

“And wild and high the Cameron’s gathering rose, The war-note of Lochiel, which Albyn’s hills have heard, And heard, too, have her Saxon foes.”

How the “Cameron men” fought at Waterloo is testified to by the number of their killed and wounded in that battle, and it is also recorded that, when all the field officers and captains of this regt. had been disabled, the regt. was led on to victory by Lieut. Cameron, a nephew of Sir Alan Cameron, the col.-in-chf.; but which of the _four_ lieutenants of this name cannot now be traced. On the evening of 18th June, 1815, 9 officers, 21 sergts., 7 drummers and 260 rank and file remained unwounded out of a total of 41 combatant officers, 40 sergts., 11 drummers, and 684 rank and file—the effective strength of the regt. at Quatre Bras.

The heroic Fassifern, great-grandson of John Cameron, 18th of Lochiel, and one of the six children of Ewen Cameron of Inverscadale, on Loch Linnhe, by his first wife, Lucy Campbell, of Balmadine. In early life was articled to a Writer to the Signet at Edinburgh; but when war broke out, in 1793, his military tastes inclined him to forsake the pen for a sword. By desire of his family, Cameron’s body was aftds. disinterred and removed to Scotland, where it was re-interred in Kilmallie churchyard, where a tall obelisk, with an inscription by Sir Walter Scott, marks his grave. An interesting memoir of this gallant soldier appeared in the _United Service Journal_ for 1837. He was a native of Dumfriesshire, where his father had a small property of his own. In 1805 he joined the 52nd L.I. as an ensign, and in the year following was appointed to a lieutenancy in the Rifle Brigade (as the old 95th is now styled). As a lieut. he had the good fortune to command one of the four companies of the Rifles which, under Sir S. Beckwith, at the Pass of Barba del Puerco, on 19th March, 1810, so gallantly repulsed 600 chosen French troops who attempted to surprise them at midnight. I extract the following from the above memoir:—“On the 19th Jan., 1812, he was one of the officers who volunteered and led the stormers at the taking of Ciudad Rodrigo, and was fortunate enough to come out unscathed, although one of the first to enter that deadly pass. At the storming of Badajoz on the 6th April, 1812, his name again stood on the list of volunteers for the Forlorn Hope, but as it was claimed by a senior officer of the division, he was obliged to limit his expectations to one of the posts of honour with the storming party. Sir Andrew Barnard, however, who commanded the Light Division, knowing how peculiarly well qualified he was for desperate enterprise, assigned him a post in front of the Forlorn Hope, in the command of a party carrying ropes prepared with nooses to throw over the sword-blades which formed the chevaux-de-frise, in the hope of being able to displace it by dragging it down the breach, but Johnstone and all his party were stricken down before they got within throwing distance. His appearance next morning is thus described by a brother officer, Capt. Kincaid, in _Random Shots from a Rifleman_, page 287:—‘The first tent that I entered was Johnstone’s. With his shattered arm bandaged, he was lying fast asleep, and coupling his appearance with the daring duty he had been called on to perform but a few hours before in front of the Forlorn Hope, I thought that I had never set my eyes upon a nobler picture of a soldier! His whole appearance, even in sleep, showed exactly as it had been in the execution of that duty; his splendid figure was so disposed as if he was taking the first step in the breach—his eyebrows were elevated—his nostrils still distended, and altogether he looked as if he would clutch the castle in his remaining hand! No one could have seen him at that moment without saying—There lies a hero!’” Johnstone was wounded both at Quatre Bras and Waterloo. Promoted maj. 24th Dec., 1829. Quitted the service in 1831. In half an hour or so he heard the distant sound of action, and it approached nearer and nearer, until he heard it close beside him; and he wondered rather that he was not invited to take a share in it, when, pat to his thought, up came an aide-de-camp at full speed, telling him that Gen. Somebody ordered him to bring up his guns. The officer asked, ‘Did not the order come from Lord Wellington?’ The aide-de-camp said ‘No,’ but from the gen., whoever he was. Three weeks after his arrest he was restored to the command of his battery, to the great joy of the whole army in Spain, and after the battle of the Bidassoa he was promoted bt. maj. # Close Reading of *The Waterloo Roll Call* by Charles Dalton

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text does not present narrative "scenes" in the conventional literary sense; rather, it unfolds as an organizational and documentary structure. The book opens with a **transcriber's note** explaining that italics are represented with underscores and that minor printer's errors have been corrected. This editorial framing establishes the text as a careful historical document requiring typographical precision.

The **title page** then presents the work as "THE WATERLOO ROLL CALL. WITH BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES AND ANEcdotES" by Charles Dalton, F.R.G.S., identifying the author as a prolific military historian who has published works on the Wrays of Glentworth, General Sir Edward Cecil, and Captain John Dalton, among others. The second edition is noted as "REVISED AND ENLARGED," published in 1904 by Eyre and Spottiswoode, Government and General Publishers.

A **dedication** follows: "TO GEORGE TANCRED, ESQUIRE (LATE CAPTAIN SCOTS GREYS), OF WEENS, ROXBURGHSHIRE." This dedication connects the author to a Waterloo veteran, establishing Dalton's personal investment in the subject matter and suggesting the work emerged from relationships with participants.

The **Preface to the Second Edition** (dated September 1st, 1904) explains that time has not diminished interest in Waterloo because it is "indissolubly connected with Napoleon—the greatest master of the art of war the world has ever known." Dalton acknowledges receiving additional information from relatives of Waterloo officers, notably utilizing the annotated copy of the late Mr. J.W. O'Brien of the British Museum Library. The preface highlights as a "special feature" the inclusion of non-commissioned officers and men who served at Waterloo and subsequently received commissions.

The **Contents** section reveals the work's architecture: Part I contains the Staff lists and biographical memoirs, the British and Hanoverian Army organization, annotated lists of regiments engaged at Waterloo, medical staff, and lists of the Reserve. Part II offers a Muster Roll of the Scots Greys. Part III lists Non-Commissioned Officers who received commissions. Part IV presents "A few Waterloo Heroes," followed by an Appendix and Index.

The **Introduction to the First Edition** constitutes the text's longest continuous prose section. It opens with the epigraph "Ah! Je les tiens donc, ces Anglais!" (Now I have them at last, these English!) attributed to Napoleon. The introduction traces British fear of Napoleon from 1802 to 1814, citing a 1803 pamphlet titled *Important Considerations for the People of this Kingdom* that appealed to national resistance. The text recounts British military preparations, including the 300,000 volunteers enrolled and the expansion of army and navy. It narrates Napoleon's military triumphs (Austerlitz 1805, campaigns through 1812), the British expeditions to the Peninsula under Sir John Moore (who died at Corunna) and Sir Arthur Wellesley (who became Duke of Wellington). The introduction explains that by 1815, "of Wellington's 106,000 barely one-third were British"—the remainder consisting of King's German Legion, Hanoverian Levies, Brunswick Contingent, Nassau Contingent, Dutch and Belgian Troops. A significant portion discusses the German Legion's praises, the Hanoverian levies' conduct (noting one regiment's refusal to charge), the Brunswick Contingent's disadvantage after losing their leader at Quatre Bras, and the uselessness of Nassau, Dutch, and Belgian troops who had recently served Napoleon and believed Wellington would be defeated. The introduction provides a detailed enumeration of Napoleon's army—approximately 128,000 veterans—and his excellent subordinate commanders (Ney, Kellermann, Count Lobau). Wellington's assessment that Napoleon's presence was "fully equivalent to an additional force of 30,000 men" is quoted. The section concludes with acknowledgment of Prussian co-operation as essential to victory.

The **Abbreviations** section follows, explaining codes such as "Par." for Peninsular, "K." for Killed, "W." for Wounded, and numerous orders (G.C.H., K.C.H., K.H., etc.).

The **Staff section** begins with Commander-in-Chief Arthur, Duke of Wellington, and proceeds through military secretaries, aides-de-camp, generals, lieutenant-generals, major-generals, the Adjutant-General, Deputy Adjutant-General, Assistant Adjutants-General, the Deputy Judge Advocate, Deputy Quartermaster-General, Assistant Quartermasters-General, and the Commandant at Headquarters. Each entry includes the officer's name, rank, regiment, and sometimes notation of being wounded (W.) or killed (K.).

Following the staff list, the text provides **biographical memoirs** for each staff officer. These entries are substantial prose passages describing each officer's family background, military career, specific actions at Waterloo, post-war life, and death. For example, Lord Fitzroy Somerset's entry describes him as "youngest son of Henry, 5th Duke of Beaufort," notes his role as Wellington's "right hand" throughout Spain and Portugal, describes how he "lost his right arm at Waterloo, from a shot fired from the top of La Haye Sainte farmhouse after its capture by the French," and records his subsequent career as F.-M. Lord Raglan, Commander-in-Chief in the Crimea, where he died in 1855.

The **British and Hanoverian Army** section presents the organization "as formed in Divisions and Brigades on the 18th June, 1815." It begins with Cavalry commanded by Lieutenant-General the Earl of Uxbridge, listing seven cavalry brigades with their commanding officers and constituent regiments. The Infantry follows, organized by division (First through Sixth), each with its commanding officer, brigades, and constituent regiments with their lieutenant-colonels or majors.

The **Regimental Lists** begin with 1st Life Guards and proceed through numerous cavalry and infantry regiments. Each regiment's section presents a table with columns for rank in the regiment and army rank, followed by footnotes that expand into lengthy biographical entries. The text breaks off partway through the 95th Regiment of Foot (Riflemen), with the final entries being the Royal Staff Corps and Royal Wagon Train, including Royal Artillery details with troop assignments.

## 2. Characters Who Speak or Act, and What Drives Them

Although *The Waterloo Roll Call* is fundamentally a reference work rather than a narrative, the text contains numerous historical figures whose actions, words, and motivations are documented. The character who dominates the text both as subject and as cited authority is **Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington**. His character emerges through his commands, his quoted assessment of Napoleon ("fully equivalent to an additional force of 30,000 men"), his quoted statement to Earl Stanhope about time, and numerous references to his leadership. Dalton presents Wellington as "a heaven-born general" (echoing Pitt's earlier assessment of Clive), whose "fame far exceeded the many titles he won by his genius." The biographical entries consistently reference officers' relations to Wellington—whether as his staff, as commanders under his orders, or as objects of his acknowledgment. Wellington's character is defined by his military genius, his demanding standards, and his role as the focal point of the British military apparatus at Waterloo.

The text's other primary character is **Napoleon Bonaparte**, presented as the great antagonist whose "marvellous power" had subjugated Europe. His presence at Waterloo is treated as a force multiplier, and the text notes his tactical superiority in "rapid and offensive warfare." Napoleon's quoted exclamation upon seeing the British army—"Ah! Je les tiens donc, ces Anglais!" (Now I have them at last, these English!)—captures his confidence before the battle.

**The Earl of Uxbridge** (later Marquis of Anglesey) appears as the cavalry commander, described as "The Prince Murat of the British Army." His brilliant handling of cavalry at Waterloo is recorded, as is his wounding ("Wounded in the right knee during the last charge; his right leg was amputated after the battle"). The text includes an anecdote about his leg being buried under a tree with a verse: "Here lies the Marquis of Anglesey's leg; / Pray for the rest of his body, I beg."

**Sir Thomas Picton** is presented as the leader of "the 'fighting' third division in the Peninsular War." The text describes how he "received a probably mortal wound at Quatre Bras but concealed the fact... in order that he might be present at what he foresaw was to be a tremendous struggle." He fell "gloriously leading a charge of infantry to repel one of the most serious attacks made by the enemy on our position." The text notes Napoleon's query on the morning of June 18th: "_Où est la division de Picton?_" and observes that "a few hours later, the broken ranks and decimated companies of many French regts. answered the question."

**Lord Hill** is presented as "the 2nd son and 4th child of a family of sixteen," who entered the 53rd Regiment as lieutenant in 1793 and distinguished himself at Arroyo and Almaraz. His quote from a letter to his sister—"'I verily believe there never was so tremendous a battle fought as that at Waterloo'"—reveals his sense of the battle's magnitude.

Among staff officers, **Lord Fitzroy Somerset** (later Lord Raglan) emerges as Wellington's principal military secretary and "right hand." His loss of his right arm at Waterloo, his subsequent career, and his death at Sebastopol during the Crimean War are detailed. His character is defined by his close relationship with Wellington and his ultimate fate as a commander in another famous campaign.

**Sir Colin Campbell** (later Lord Clyde) appears as a young officer who "ran away from Perth Academy" in 1792 and entered service as a midshipman before rising to high command. His anecdote about being captured at Kingston, Jamaica, by his brother Patrick (an admiral) and being brought home illustrates his adventurous early career. His later command in the Crimea and death in 1847 complete his trajectory.

**Colonel Sir William Howe De Lancey** is presented with extensive biographical detail, including his marriage "in Scotland, in April, 1815, to the beautiful Magdalen Hall, dau. of Sir James Hall, Bart., of Dunglass." His death at Waterloo—"when riding by Wellington's side, the wind of a cannon ball knocked him off his horse. This... had separated the ribs from the back-bone, and caused a fatal injury"—is narrated with particular pathos. His widow's experiences driving to the battlefield and nursing him are noted as recently published from her manuscript narrative.

The text documents hundreds of regimental officers, each with individual biographical entries. Many entries reveal character through anecdote: **Captain Horace Beauchamp Seymour** is described as "the strongest man in the British Army," who is said to have "slain more men at Waterloo than any other single individual." His capture and rescue by Wellington's cavalry is recorded, and he is identified as the original of "Capt. Trevanion" in Charles Lever's *Harry Lorrequer*, with a detailed anecdote about his confrontation with a French bully in Paris after Waterloo.

**Captain Thomas Wildman** is noted as having "purchased the Newstead Abbey estate for £95,000 from Mr. Clawton, who had bought it of Lord Byron for £14,000," revealing his wealth and connection to literary history.

**Sir Colquhoun Grant** appears with extended biographical treatment, including a lengthy anecdote about his service at Clonmel where he gave offense to "an honest shopkeeper, named Mulcahy, who struck him on the parade." Rather than having Mulcahy arrested, Grant declared he had been the aggressor and agreed to fight with "fists only," subsequently defeating Mulcahy in the mess-room. This anecdote reveals Grant's sense of honor and preference for personal resolution over formal proceedings.

**Captain James John Fraser** is noted as "afterwards Sir James John Fraser, Bart.," who "succeeded his brother, Sir Wm. Fraser, in 1827" and was "a direct descendant of 1st Lord Lovat."

What drives these characters, as presented in the text, is a combination of military ambition, sense of duty, family honor, and sometimes personal vendetta or revenge. The biographical entries consistently trace officers' motivations to family tradition (many are sons or nephews of previous military men), personal ambition (entering service young, seeking distinction), and sense of duty (serving despite wounds, continuing after injury).

## 3. Four Passages Worth Quoting

**Passage 1:**
> "Ah! Je les tiens donc, ces Anglais!"—NAPOLEON.

This epigraph, placed before the Introduction, captures Napoleon's confidence upon seeing the British army drawn up at Waterloo. The French phrase establishes the international context of the campaign while revealing Napoleon's psychological state—triumphant, eager, convinced of victory. The attribution to Napoleon creates a framing device that positions the entire Roll Call as a response to his challenge. The text will document, officer by officer, how those English were indeed "held" but not conquered.

**Passage 2:**
> "Since the publication of my ROLL CALL in 1890, I have received much additional information from the relatives of Waterloo officers. This has enabled me to bring out the present revised and enlarged edition."

From the Preface to the Second Edition, this passage reveals Dalton's methodology: his work emerges from active engagement with descendants of Waterloo participants, creating a network of familial knowledge transmission. The phrase "relatives of Waterloo officers" suggests a form of memorialization driven by family pride and historical obligation. The "additional information" implies that initial publication was incomplete, establishing the Roll Call as a work perpetually under revision, never fully complete.

**Passage 3:**
> "Of Wellington's 106,000 barely one-third were British. The remainder consisted of 'King's German Legion,' 'Hanoverian Levies,' 'Brunswick Contingent,' 'Nassau Contingent,' 'Dutch and Belgian Troops,' and 'Nassauers in Dutch service.' Of this polyglot force the German Legion, both cavalry and infantry, were deserving of the highest praise for their conduct on Waterloo Day."

This passage from the Introduction reveals the multinational nature of Wellington's force and establishes the text's scope—the Roll Call will document primarily British officers, but the Introduction acknowledges the complex coalition involved. The phrase "polyglot force" suggests both linguistic and cultural diversity. The special praise for the German Legion introduces a theme of reliable foreign troops contrasted with unreliable ones (the Hanoverian regiment that "refused to charge" and the Belgian troops who "preferred making a 'retrograde movement for strategical reasons'").

**Passage 4:**
> "He had five horses shot under him at Waterloo. G.C.B., G.C.H. Col.-in-Chf. 15th Hussars, 1827. Lt.-Gen. Succeeded to a large property at Frampton, co. Dorset, 1833. M. Marcia, dau. of Rev. J. Richards, of Long Bredy, co. Dorset, and had an only surviving child, Marcia, who eloped with Richard Brinsley Sheridan in May 1835."

This biographical footnote for Sir Colquhoun Grant encapsulates the typical arc of a Waterloo officer's life: distinguished service (five horses killed under him), honors (G.C.B., G.C.H.), career advancement (Colonelcy, Lieutenant-General), property acquisition, marriage, and a dramatic final detail (his daughter's elopement with Richard Brinsley Sheridan). The passage demonstrates how biographical details in the Roll Call extend far beyond military service, situating officers within broader social and familial narratives. The elopement transforms the military record into a window onto Regency society.

## 4. Themes and How Prose Builds Them

The text develops several interconnected themes through its archival structure and biographical methodology.

**The Diversity of Wellington's Army**: The text repeatedly emphasizes that Waterloo was not merely a British victory but a coalition effort. The Introduction explicitly states that "barely one-third" of Wellington's force was British, and the army organization tables reveal regiments from Hanover, Brunswick, Nassau, and the King's German Legion participating. This theme establishes the battle as a multinational effort and justifies the text's scope (focusing on British officers while acknowledging foreign contributions). The prose builds this theme through enumeration and contrast—the reliable German Legion is praised while Belgian and Dutch troops are characterized as faithless.

**The Biographical Depth of Military History**: The text transforms what could be a dry roster into a collection of human stories. Each officer's entry includes not just dates and ranks but family background, military career, specific actions, wounds, and post-war lives. This biographical approach treats officers as full human subjects rather than military functions. The prose builds this theme through accumulated detail: the narrative for Colonel De Lancey includes his marriage, his wife's journey to the battlefield, his ten-day death, and his burial; the entry for Captain Seymour includes his reputation as "the strongest man" and his fictionalized appearance in Lever's novel. Each footnote becomes a life history compressed into a few sentences.
